messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Imani has worked the same plot of land for over fifty years, her hands intimately familiar with the pull of a stubborn weed and the texture of rich, dark soil. At seventy-four, she still found a deep satisfaction in the rhythm of the seasons. That was, until last spring. The attack happened just as dusk was settling, in the quiet rows of late-season tomatoes. She was alone, enjoying the cool air after a hot day, when he had come out of nowhere. The world had gone completely, terrifyingly still; there was no birdsong, no wind, just the sound of her own breathing and then his. The most visceral part of the memory was the smell of the damp, freshly turned earth as her face was pressed into it, a scent that had once meant life and sustenance but now only heralded terror.

In the months that followed, Imani’s world shrank. The feeling of being contaminated became a constant companion. She would spend hours in the shower, scrubbing her skin until it was raw, but the sense of being soiled was internal, a stain on her very soul that no soap could reach. She came to believe her body was a source of shame, something ruined and defiled. This belief became a wall between her and Samuel, her partner of two decades. When he would reach for her hand, a simple gesture of affection they had shared thousands oftimes, she would flinch away as if from a hot iron. The hurt in his eyes was a constant mirror to her own self-loathing, but she couldn’t explain that letting him touch her felt like spreading the contamination, like poisoning the one good thing she had left. Any physical contact, even an accidental brush in the kitchen, sent a jolt of panic through her.

Her work, once her sanctuary, became a place of perpetual ambush. Every morning, the rich, loamy smell of the fields would hit her, and the memory would rush back, not as a thought but as a full-body experience. She would feel the phantom weight on her back, the grit of dirt in her mouth. To cope, she developed a fierce, silent ritual. “Think of the sun, think of the harvest, think of good things,” she would repeat to herself, forcing a litany of positive thoughts into her mind to drown out the images. It was an exhausting battle she fought from sunrise to sunset. The nights offered no relief. Darkness itself felt threatening, a blanket under which anything could hide. She began leaving lights on in every room of their small house, unable to bear the thought of being enveloped by the same blackness that had covered her that evening.

Now, with the one-year anniversary of the assault just weeks away, the fragile defenses she has built are crumbling. The silence in the house after Samuel goes to bed has become deafening, a vacuum that pulls the memories right out of her. The intrusive thoughts are more frequent, her forced positivity failing against their onslaught. The shame has curdled into a deep, weary despair. More and more, she finds herself looking at her long life, at the calloused hands that have tended the earth and raised a family, and thinking that this ending is an unbearable cruelty. The thought, once a whisper, has grown louder: she is not sure her life is worth living anymore. It was after she finally voiced this fear to Samuel, her voice cracking in the brightly lit kitchen at 2 a.m., that he made the call. Imani is here now, not with any real hope, but out of a promise to him. What she fears most is that the feeling of being dirty is permanent, but what she quietly wishes for is to one day stand in her garden, breathe in the smell of the earth, and feel nothing at all.
